entries.text: Iranian IRGC-affiliated cyber actors (CyberAv3ngers, APT33, APT55) are almost certainly conducting active cyber operations against U.S. critical infrastructure in retaliation for Operation Epic Fury, with Texas Gulf Coast energy infrastructure assessed as a priority target given the strategic significance of Permian Basin and LNG export infrastructure.

China's Volt Typhoon/Voltzite very likely maintains persistent access inside at least one U.S. critical-infrastructure network connected to the electric grid and is almost certainly positioned to cause disruption in a future conflict scenario; ERCOT, despite defeating a known 2024 Volt Typhoon breach attempt, likely faces continued reconnaissance.

The IRGC's March 2026 drone strikes against AWS data centers in the UAE and Bahrain represent a strategic precedent highly likely to reshape how Iran, Russia, and China conceptualize commercial cloud infrastructure as a legitimate military target, elevating risk for Texas organizations relying on cloud-hosted OT and financial-clearinghouse infrastructure.

Russia's GRU-linked Sandworm (Electrum/Kamacite) likely remains postured for opportunistic escalation against U.S. energy infrastructure should the Iran conflict create a strategic window, demonstrating a standing collection posture rather than a dormant one.

The Ras Laffan LNG terminal strikes of 18-19 March 2026 and associated Gulf energy attacks will likely drive LNG price volatility and supply-chain disruption for Texas Gulf Coast operators within 30-60 days, with roughly even chances of follow-on IRGC-affiliated cyber operations.

Handala, a confirmed MOIS-operated persona, almost certainly will continue offensive cyber operations against U.S. targets regardless of U.S. government domain seizures; DomainTools confirmed Handala reconstituted domains within hours of the DOJ's March 19 seizure, stating 'We decided to respond to their seizure.'

The Stryker attack methodology (credential compromise via infostealer, AD privilege escalation, mass device wipe via Microsoft Intune) very likely represents a replicable playbook now available to multiple MOIS-affiliated actors; Texas healthcare, energy, and defense-contractor organizations using Intune-managed Microsoft 365 face elevated exposure.

The Patel Gmail breach reveals a persistent Iranian long-cycle collection operation against U.S. national-security officials that almost certainly predates the current conflict; NBC News reporting confirms the emails were organized into folders last modified in May 2025, nine months before the current war.

Handala's operational pattern of targeting life-critical sectors, using supply-chain footholds, and following attacks with propaganda likely signals that Texas Medical Center ecosystem vendors and mid-tier Texas healthcare suppliers are higher-probability targets than large hospital networks directly.

Iran's cyber doctrine is almost certainly executing along three simultaneous tracks: destructive state operations (Stryker wiper), hack-and-leak influence operations (Patel Gmail), and ongoing ICS/OT reconnaissance against energy and critical infrastructure; Texas faces exposure across all three tracks.

Cyber risk is almost certainly migrating from data exposure toward operational disruption, as evidenced by Hasbro's disclosure that a March 28 intrusion forced systems offline and may delay fulfillment for weeks; the SEC 8-K disclosure pattern is becoming standard for material cyber events.

The LiteLLM/Trivy supply-chain compromise very likely represents the leading edge of a sustained extortion wave targeting AI-dependent organizations; TeamPCP's partnership with Lapsus$ mirrors the 2023 MOVEit campaign pattern, with Texas technology, financial-services, and defense contractors as probable follow-on targets.

Russian-linked actors are likely conducting systematic return operations against previously breached networks, per CERT-UA's April 3 report, revisiting prior footholds to test whether access persists and patched vulnerabilities have been re-exposed; a breach resolved in 2024/2025 may not be closed.

Healthcare almost certainly remains the sector most structurally exposed to both data theft and operational disruption; the Nacogdoches Memorial Hospital disclosure (257,073 individuals affected, attacker present Jan 15-31 before detection) illustrates 16-day dwell times occurring without visible indicators in Texas regional hospitals.

Iranian-affiliated cyber actors are almost certainly expanding disruptive OT targeting against U.S. energy and water infrastructure, and Texas falls into the highest-risk tier given its concentration of Gulf Coast petrochemical, utility, and water-treatment environments. Primary uncertainty: open reporting does not yet name Texas victims.

PRC Typhoon actors very likely retain dormant access inside U.S. critical-infrastructure and telecommunications ecosystems; the greatest near-term danger for Texas is not immediate disruption but silent compromise that reduces warning time in a future crisis.

DPRK financial cyber operations will almost certainly continue at scale through 2026; Texas financial institutions with crypto, fintech, or DeFi-adjacent exposure face elevated third-party and integration risk. The Drift theft demonstrated DPRK actors can execute nine-figure thefts at machine speed once access is established.

Ransomware actors will likely increase supply-chain and identity-first attacks against Texas healthcare and DIB targets through Q2/Q3 2026, compressing time between vulnerability disclosure and operational impact.

Reduced federal cyber capacity will likely increase the intelligence and response burden on private organizations, raising the value of commercial warning, internal detection maturity, and direct state-level coordination for Texas decision-makers.

North Korea's use of AI to conduct social engineering against individuals with privileged access to financial systems and technology infrastructure will almost certainly continue to intensify through 2026; Texas financial institutions, fintech operators, and technology companies are inside the operational target profile.

Iran's demonstrated willingness to generate operational disruption against U.S. industrial infrastructure, confirmed in a joint federal advisory, very likely represents a persistent posture, not a temporary campaign; Texas energy and water operators remain in the highest-risk tier while the U.S.-Iran confrontation remains unresolved.

PRC Typhoon actors very likely retain dormant access inside U.S. critical-infrastructure and telecommunications ecosystems, and the strategic value of that access increases as U.S.-China competition over Taiwan and technology accelerates; the risk to Texas grows with geopolitical tension.

Operation PowerOFF's disruption of criminal denial-of-service infrastructure will likely produce a near-term rebound in disruptive activity, consistent with historical pattern; Texas financial services, healthcare portals, and public-facing critical infrastructure should treat the next 30 days as elevated availability risk.

The federal government's permanent narrowing of its national vulnerability intelligence program likely creates a structural intelligence gap for Texas organizations without supplemental threat intelligence sources, increasing the probability that high-impact enterprise software vulnerabilities go unaddressed.

Texas AI and data-center infrastructure growth is almost certainly transitioning from a commercial development story into a strategic cyber-terrain issue; ERCOT grid reliability, Houston-area industrial load concentration, and behind-the-meter energy dependencies will become increasingly attractive targets for state-sponsored pre-positioning through 2026-2027.

Third-party vendor compromise is likely the most probable near-term pathway for significant cyber-related financial and reputational harm to Texas banking and financial institutions; 'our network was not breached' will not constitute an adequate defense following a vendor-linked incident.

North Korean IT-worker insertion schemes almost certainly represent a live insider-adjacent risk to U.S. technology, defense, AI, and financial-sector organizations, including those in Texas; DOJ sentencing and Treasury sanctions this month signal sustained enforcement attention but not elimination of the threat.

Iranian cyber actors likely remain in a posture of active capability development and selective OT disruption; Texas energy, water, and petrochemical operators using internet-exposed PLCs remain inside the highest-risk tier even as advisory-driven headline attention recedes.

Pro-Russian cyber groups are likely deliberately escalating from denial-of-service nuisance operations toward attempted destructive cyberattacks against critical infrastructure in Europe, a leading indicator of what Russia's cyber-adjacent ecosystem may bring to U.S. infrastructure as geopolitical friction intensifies.

It is likely (55-80%) that CI Fortify guidance forms the basis for sector-specific regulatory expectations applicable to Texas energy, water, and healthcare operators within 12-18 months, via state regulators, Texas DIR, ERCOT reliability standards, and CMS conditions of participation.

There is an even chance (40-55%) that at least one publicly disclosed agentic AI security incident affecting a Texas data center, hyperscaler tenant, or downstream enterprise customer becomes public within the next 6-9 months.

It is likely (55-80%) that at least one publicly named DPRK IT-worker victim company in the next six months will be Texas-headquartered, given more than 100 historically named victim companies and the concentration of remote technical hiring across Austin, Dallas, and Houston.

entries.text: It is likely (55-80%) that Iranian OT-targeting tempo against U.S. water and energy operators persists at the current elevated baseline through at least the end of Q3 2026; the 7 April joint advisory has not been retired or downgraded and the conflict environment has not resolved in a de-escalatory direction.

It is almost certain (95-99%) that perimeter edge devices (VPN, firewall, gateway) remain the dominant ransomware initial-access vector against Texas mid-market manufacturers, healthcare practices, and DIB suppliers through the remainder of 2026.

It is likely (55-80%) that Texas infrastructure concentration itself -- AI compute load, ERCOT grid dependency, telecom corridor concentration, and MSP/cloud access consolidation -- has become a strategic objective for nation-state adversary pre-positioning.
It is likely (55-80%) that Texas healthcare cyber risk will increasingly manifest as operational continuity and patient-safety risk, not only data-protection risk.
It is likely (55-80%) that ERCOT grid stress during summer 2026 will create exploitable operational vulnerability windows if cyber, physical, and vendor-continuity plans remain separated.

It is highly likely (>80%) that Iran's wartime cyber campaign is in an active, multi-vector operational phase, not a pre-positioning or background collection phase: confirmed PLC disruption (CISA AA26-097a), suspected ATG infrastructure access, and active human-capital targeting of aviation and oil-and-gas software engineers (Unit 42, 22 May) constitute an escalating operational pattern.

It is likely (55-80%) that the convergence of Iran-war energy price shocks and AI-driven electricity demand has created a dual-vector energy stress environment that adversaries can exploit, and that Texas governance structures are not currently calibrated to manage simultaneously. (Labeled MODERATE-HIGH CONFIDENCE in source, styled as Moderate.)

It is likely (55-80%) that AI-enabled adversary operations have outpaced the identity and access governance frameworks most Texas enterprises currently operate under, creating a category of cyber risk that does not fit conventional IT security models and is already being operationalized against U.S. organizations.
It is very likely (80-95%) that Iranian coercion of Hormuz undersea cable infrastructure will escalate from fee-assertion to active interference before a negotiated resolution is reached.

It is likely (55-80%) that ERCOT grid stress during summer 2026, compounded by AI data-center load concentration, will create exploitable operational vulnerability windows if cyber and physical continuity plans remain separated.

It is likely (55-80%) that China-linked infrastructure persistence represents a pre-conflict access strategy that will be activated against U.S. critical infrastructure during a future Taiwan or regional crisis, and Texas energy, telecom, and AI/data-center infrastructure are inside that targeting set.

Texas energy and logistics infrastructure faces elevated operational risk this summer from the intersection of confirmed adversary OT targeting, ERCOT grid instability pressure, and the dependency gap between how fast AI and crypto load is connecting and how its grid behavior is modeled.

entries.text: Russian government hackers will keep breaking into routers and network equipment that still have factory-default settings, and Texas organizations with older equipment or informal IT management carry the same risk demonstrated this week.

The weak point isn't routers alone -- it's any equipment that sits on the edge of the network and connects to the internet, including systems employees use for remote access; a second, unrelated attacker proved this the same week by exploiting a critical SonicWall SMA1000 flaw.

Having a security-contact email posted on a website is not the same as having a working process. Organizations that haven't tested how an outside report reaches a real decision-maker risk the same failure that just happened to CISA's own vulnerability-disclosure process.

Carried forward from ATB-2026-17/18: Iran likely still wants to retaliate against U.S. infrastructure with a cyberattack, and this week's confirmed U.S. combat deaths in Jordan and Iraq make that motive stronger -- but there is still no evidence an actual cyberattack has happened. (MODERATE CONFIDENCE, UNCHANGED.)
